title: Waller sets out a December hike preference and a test for going further
summary: Before the October consumer price release, Governor Christopher Waller favoured a 25-basis-point December increase even if monthly inflation improved. A third reading near 0.3 percent or higher for monthly core CPI would lead him to consider 50 basis points. He explained that he had supported October’s hold because communication about the future path had already tightened financial conditions. In his view, consecutive moves were unnecessary, but failing to deliver within a reasonable period could undo the tightening as markets revised their expectations. This was Waller’s own contingent preference, not a December vote or a report of the October CPI outcome.

His inflation analysis focused on how many prices were rising quickly and which components were doing so. September PCE inflation was 0.5 percent for the month and 3.7 percent over twelve months. Core PCE rose 0.3 and 3.1 percent over the same intervals. Waller placed less weight on earlier pressure in prices that statisticians must impute and more on increases in goods and market-based services excluding housing. More than 70 percent of core PCE services components had twelve-month increases above 3 percent. That is a share of components, not the share of household expenditure exposed to those increases.

He identified two possible sources of persistence. Price-pressure measures constructed from purchasing managers’ named inputs had anticipated some high-tech producer price increases, and the October survey suggested more might follow. Separately, research cited in the speech suggested that energy costs might pass into core prices for longer than before the pandemic. Costs of shipping and insuring oil and limits on diesel refining could sustain pressure even if crude prices retreated. These are competing sources of inflation news, with no numerical decomposition presented in the speech. Waller cited reports putting the additional cost associated with insurance and transfers between vessels at $20–30 a barrel. He did not present that estimate as a change in the futures price. For diesel users, limited refining capacity could keep delivered fuel expensive even after crude eased. His example of the purchasing-managers index also had a specific lag: high-tech input pressure emerged in December 2025, intensified in January and subsequently showed up in February producer prices. The October survey provided an early warning. It supplied no forecast coefficient for the PCE index (notes 5–7).

On activity, Waller cited the initial 3.4 percent third-quarter real GDP growth estimate. October payrolls rose by 165,000, previous months were revised upward by 85,000 in total, and unemployment was 4.1 percent. Both six- and twelve-month average payroll gains were nearer 80,000. Under these conditions he judged the level of employment close to maximum, supporting his near-term focus on prices.

His longer-run labour diagnosis was less settled. September’s net gain of 60,000 jobs sat alongside more than five million hires and more than five million separations. The accompanying JOLTS tables put the September hiring and separation rates at 3.4 and 3.3 percent of nonfarm employment respectively. Low turnover can reflect a population with more older or highly educated workers, improved matches from earlier job switching, or barriers preventing workers from reaching higher-productivity firms. These explanations imply different potential output paths. Waller cited longer unemployment spells and difficulties facing new entrants as reasons to investigate the last possibility. He expressly left that diagnosis open. The distribution of unemployment provides a cross-check. The three-month average share of unemployed people out of work for at least 27 weeks rose from about 18% at the end of 2022 to above 27% through September 2026 (note 4). Joblessness can last longer for those who lose work even as fewer people enter unemployment. Waller also suggested a testable alternative: the pandemic job switchers may have found unusually good matches, or simply have yet to reach the roughly three years he gave as typical tenure before another move.

An event study needs the London speech timestamp and the subsequent U.S. CPI release. The speech placed a condition on an observation still in the future. Assigning the day’s full movement in yields to the remarks would combine the announcement of his condition with the news determining whether traders thought it had been met.

questions.question: Was the December alternative already priced before the speech?
questions.detail: Compare contracts settling around the December meeting and options on those rates immediately before and after the speech, stopping the first window before CPI. Then examine the separate price-release window. A change in the odds of a larger move may alter the shape of the distribution more than its average.

questions.question: Did broad services inflation signal persistence or a base effect?
questions.detail: Reconstruct Waller’s count of components above 3 percent using unchanged definitions, then compare expenditure-weighted breadth, shorter annualised changes and measures excluding imputed prices. A twelve-month count can stay high after near-term momentum has slowed.

questions.question: Does reduced labour turnover indicate better matches or barriers to mobility?
questions.detail: Estimate hiring, separations, wage gains after job changes and unemployment duration by age, education and tenure. Stable jobs with stronger productivity and pay would support the match-quality interpretation. Persistently weak entry rates and deteriorating wage progression would support a different explanation.

questions.question: How quickly did balance-sheet supply pressures feed into PCE prices?
questions.detail: Follow purchase-manager reports for individual inputs through corresponding producer prices into downstream consumer categories. Compare energy-intensive and less exposed services. A leading survey signal is evidence about timing, while the magnitude of pass-through requires measured prices and expenditure weights.
